summary.title: Concurrent Servers: Part 4 - libuv
summary.one_liner: Learn how libuv wraps an event loop for concurrent C servers, how to offload blocking work to its thread pool, and how it makes file-system calls asynchronous.
takeaways: libuv hides platform-specific event loops (epoll, etc.) behind a portable API where you register callbacks and run the loop.
Long-running work in a callback blocks the whole event loop; moving it to the libuv thread pool via uv_queue_work keeps the loop responsive.
Pass custom state into libuv callbacks through the handle's data field, and manage heap memory carefully because callbacks run on different stack frames.
libuv's file-system functions are asynchronous because they submit blocking POSIX calls as work items to the thread pool when a callback is given.
summary.summary: This is part 4 of a series on writing concurrent network servers in C. The post rewrites the protocol server using libuv, showing TCP setup, uv_listen, uv_accept, uv_write and uv_read_start callbacks, and the data-field idiom for passing state. It demonstrates how a blocking callback stalls the event loop and how uv_queue_work moves that work to a thread pool. It also walks through libuv's source (src/unix/fs.c) to show how uv_fs_read uses INIT/POST macros to run blocking file I/O on the work queue. The post ends with a primality-testing server and two exercises on blocking versus non-blocking modes and thread-pool size.
